warmup.q: A Parquet file holds 400,000 payments in 4 blocks of about 100,000 rows each, and it records the smallest and largest amount in each block. The payments were written in the order they happened, so every block holds amounts from about 1 euro to about 2,500 euros. How many blocks can a reader skip when it looks for payments above 2,400 euros?
options: Three, because only about 4% of the payments match
None, because every block's range reaches above 2,400 euros
All four, because the filter is handed to the file reader
It depends on which compressor the file uses
warmup.why: A reader skips a block only when its smallest and largest values prove that no row in it can match. Here every block's largest amount is near 2,500 euros, so each one might hold a match, and all four get read. The same rows sorted by amount let a reader skip three of the four. The share of rows that match doesn't matter, and compression doesn't change the stored values. The first option is the trap: 4% of the rows match, but they're spread across every block.

sections.h: Building a column file that one pass can write: row groups, chunks and a footer
sections.html:
Here are the payments we'll store: 400,000 rows, each with five columns. They are payment_id, merchant_id (the shop that was paid), card_country, status and amount_cents. A CSV file, plain text with commas between the values, stores each payment whole, one line after another. To add up the amounts, a reader has to read every byte of every line, the shops and the countries included.

A column file turns that around. It stores all the payment numbers together, then all the shop numbers, then all the amounts. To add up the amounts, a reader fetches one run of values and skips the rest. The Storage track's lesson Column stores and compression built this inside one database. Parquet is the same idea as a file format, so that many programs can read the same files. Spark, DuckDB and Trino all read it. Spark runs data jobs across many machines, DuckDB is a database program that runs on one computer, and Trino runs SQL over many kinds of storage. Parquet also lets a reader on S3, Amazon's online file store, fetch only the parts it needs. S3 can send a byte range, such as bytes 1,000 to 2,000 of a file, without the rest.

Let's try to design such a file ourselves.

Version 1: one long run per column. Write all 400,000 payment numbers, then all 400,000 shop numbers, and so on. This breaks on the writing side. The writer can't put down the first shop number until it has written the last payment number, so it must hold the whole table in memory first. A program writing a 10 GB file would need 10 GB of memory.

Version 2: cut the rows into slices, and store each slice column by column. Take 100,000 rows, write their payment numbers, then their shop numbers, then their amounts. Then the next 100,000. The writer now holds one slice at a time. Parquet calls a slice a row group, and one column's values inside a row group a column chunk. A file with 5 columns and 4 row groups has 20 chunks. Each chunk is stored as one or more pages, the smallest piece a reader unpacks at once.

Version 3: a reader that wants only the amounts must know where each amount chunk starts. So the writer keeps a map. For every chunk, it notes where the chunk begins, as a byte offset from the start of the file. It also notes the chunk's size, how its values are packed (its encoding, which the next section opens), and the smallest and largest value in it. The writer knows the offsets only after it has written the chunks, so it writes the map last, at the end of the file. The Parquet spec gives exactly this reason: the metadata, the data about the data, comes last "to allow for single pass writing". This map is the footer. After it come 4 bytes holding the footer's length, then the 4 letters PAR1. The file starts with PAR1 too, so a program can check that it really is Parquet.

So a reader opens a Parquet file from the back, in three steps:

  1. Read the last 8 bytes: the footer's length and PAR1.
  2. Read the footer.
  3. Read only the chunks the query needs, each as one byte range.

On S3, where every read is a request over the network, that's two small requests, then exactly the bytes the query needs. (Readers often fetch a bigger piece of the end, and get the footer with the first request.) The figure below is the picture for the whole lesson.

How big should a row group be? Bigger row groups mean longer runs per column, so fewer, larger reads. They also mean more memory in the writer. The Parquet docs recommend 512 MB to 1 GB. parquet-java, the library Spark uses to write Parquet, cuts a row group at 128 MB by default (its parquet.block.size setting). The demo asks DuckDB for 100,000 rows per group, so that a small file still has four.

Write the map last, so one pass can write the file. Read it first, so a reader can skip.

The footer tells a reader where every chunk lives. Next, we'll see how small a chunk can get.

try.title: Open a Parquet file from the back
steps: From the labs folder, run FooterDemo. It writes 400,000 payments sorted by amount to build/l04/sorted.parquet, reads the last 8 bytes by hand, and asks DuckDB to decode the footer.
Find the 4 bytes that hold the footer's length. Work out their value yourself before you read the next line.
Check one offset: does merchant_id in row group 0 start right where payment_id ends?

code.title: FooterDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l05.demo import java.io.RandomAccessFile import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.nio.ByteOrder /** Reads the end of a Parquet file by hand, then prints the map of the file its footer holds. */ fun main() { PaymentParquet.open().use { c -> val file = PaymentParquet.sorted RandomAccessFile(file, "r").use { f -> val head = ByteArray(4).also { f.readFully(it) } f.seek(f.length() - 8) val tail = ByteArray(8).also { f.readFully(it) } val footerLength = ByteBuffer.wrap(tail, 0, 4).order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).int println("file: %s, %,d bytes".format(file.name, f.length())) println("first 4 bytes: %s".format(String(head))) println("last 8 bytes: %s (%s)".format(tail.joinToString(" ") { "%02x".format(it) }, String(tail, 4, 4))) println("footer: %,d bytes, starting at byte %,d".format(footerLength, f.length() - 8 - footerLength)) } // DuckDB decodes the footer for us: one row per column chunk val chunks = c.rows( """SELECT row_group_id, row_group_num_rows, path_in_schema, data_page_offset, dictionary_page_offset, total_compressed_size, stats_min, stats_max FROM parquet_metadata('${file.absolutePath}') ORDER BY row_group_id, column_id""") for ((group, rows) in chunks.groupBy { it[0] }) { println("row group %s: %,d rows".format(group, rows[0][1]!!.toLong())) for (r in rows) { val start = minOf(r[3]!!.toLong(), r[4]?.toLong() ?: Long.MAX_VALUE) println(" %-13s at byte %,10d %,8d bytes min %-10s max %s".format(r[2], start, r[5]!!.toLong(), r[6], r[7])) } if (group == "1") { println(" ... row groups 2 and 3 look the same"); break } } } }

(Output trimmed in the middle.) The bytes 0b 09 00 00 are little-endian, which means the lowest byte comes first. Read backwards, they're 0x090b in hexadecimal (counting in base 16), which is 2,315. Each chunk starts where the one before it ended: 4 + 486,462 = 486,466. The footer is 2,315 bytes for 3.6 MB of data. DuckDB rounded 100,000 rows up to 100,352, a multiple of the 2,048-row batches it works in. The amount ranges climb from one row group to the next because this file is sorted by amount.

aside.title: Why not keep each column in a file of its own?
aside.html: You could, and some databases store each column separately inside their own storage. As shared files on S3, though, one file per column means many files to open for every query, and every file is a request with its own wait. Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore showed what many small files cost. Keeping all the columns of a slice in one file means one footer describes the whole slice. And a reader that needs a whole payment finds all five of its columns in the same row group.

sections.h: Shrinking a column before compressing it: dictionaries, runs and differences
sections.html:
The footer tells a reader where the status chunk lives. How many bytes does it take there? A status is one of four words: AUTHORIZED (the bank set the money aside), CAPTURED (the money moved), DECLINED or REFUNDED. The demo writes the same 100,352 payments several ways and measures one chunk each time. The Storage track's lesson Column stores and compression met these tricks inside a database. Here we'll see what Parquet calls them, who picks them, and what they save.

Written PLAIN, every value is stored in full: a 4-byte length, then the letters. AUTHORIZED costs 14 bytes, and the chunk of 100,352 statuses takes 1,254,547 bytes. That's 12.5 bytes a row for a column with four different values.

Writing the same four words a hundred thousand times is wasteful, and dictionary encoding stops it. The four words are stored once, at the start of the chunk, and each row stores a small number that points to its word. Four words need only 2 bits each (00, 01, 10 and 11), and Parquet packs those bits tightly. 100,352 rows times 2 bits is 25,088 bytes. The measured chunk is 25,577 bytes, almost 50 times smaller.

Now sort the rows by status. The codes come in four long runs: all the AUTHORIZED rows, then all the CAPTURED ones, and so on. Run-length encoding stores a run as "this value, this many times". The chunk shrinks to 99 bytes.

Numbers have their own trick, delta encoding (DELTA_BINARY_PACKED): store the first value, then only the differences from one value to the next. The payment numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 differ by 1 every time, and their chunk shrinks from 802,839 bytes to 469. Random amounts follow no pattern, so their differences are as big as the values, and delta encoding only takes them down to 238,907 bytes.

Encodings work on what the values mean. On top of them comes compression: a general byte squeezer such as Snappy or Zstd, the same kind of tool as a zip file, run on each page. Spark compresses Parquet with Snappy unless you set spark.sql.parquet.compression.codec. Zstd is slower to write and usually smaller: the random amounts shrink to 476,459 bytes with Snappy and 309,537 with Zstd.

Two things follow. First, the writer chooses the encodings, so its settings decide what you get. DuckDB used delta encoding only when asked for Parquet's version 2 encodings (PARQUET_VERSION V2). Second, dictionaries have a limit. A column where every value is different, such as a unique reference code for each payment, would need a dictionary as big as the column itself. So when the dictionary grows too big, the writer falls back to plain encoding.

The sorted status column hints at something bigger. Sorting changed no value, and the column got about 250 times smaller. Next, we'll see sorting do more: let a reader skip whole row groups.

code.html: package sfz.batch.l05.demo import java.io.File import java.sql.DriverManager /** * One row group of 100,352 payments, written several ways. For each column it prints the encoding * DuckDB chose and the bytes the column chunk takes in the file. */ fun main() { val file = File("build/l04/encodings.parquet").apply { parentFile.mkdirs() } DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:duckdb:").use { c -> c.createStatement().use { s -> s.execute("""CREATE TABLE p AS SELECT i AS payment_id, ['AUTHORIZED','CAPTURED','DECLINED','REFUNDED'][(hash(i + 2) % 4)::INTEGER + 1] AS status, (hash(i + 3) % 250000 + 100)::BIGINT AS amount_cents FROM range(100352) t(i)""") } fun show(label: String, column: String, order: String, options: String) { c.createStatement().use { it.execute("COPY (SELECT * FROM p ORDER BY $order) TO '${file.absolutePath}' (FORMAT parquet, $options)") } val (encoding, bytes) = c.rows("SELECT encodings, total_compressed_size FROM parquet_metadata('${file.absolutePath}') WHERE path_in_schema = '$column'").single() println(" %-36s %-20s %,10d bytes".format(label, encoding, bytes!!.toLong())) } val raw = "COMPRESSION uncompressed" println("status: 4 distinct values") show("strings, no dictionary", "status", "payment_id", "$raw, DICTIONARY_SIZE_LIMIT 1") show("dictionary + 2-bit codes", "status", "payment_id", raw) show("dictionary, rows sorted by status", "status", "status, payment_id", raw) println("payment_id: 0, 1, 2, 3, ...") show("8-byte values", "payment_id", "payment_id", raw) show("deltas (Parquet v2)", "payment_id", "payment_id", "$raw, PARQUET_VERSION V2") println("amount_cents: random") show("8-byte values", "amount_cents", "payment_id", raw) show("deltas (Parquet v2)", "amount_cents", "payment_id", "$raw, PARQUET_VERSION V2") show("8-byte values, then Snappy", "amount_cents", "payment_id", "COMPRESSION snappy") show("8-byte values, then Zstd", "amount_cents", "payment_id", "COMPRESSION zstd") } }

  dictionary, rows sorted by status    PLAIN_DICTIONARY             99 bytes

The first three lines are the dictionary story: 1.25 MB, 25 KB and 99 bytes for the same 100,352 values. PLAIN_DICTIONARY is the old name of dictionary encoding; with PARQUET_VERSION V2, DuckDB writes the newer RLE_DICTIONARY. 802,839 is 100,352 x 8 bytes plus a few bytes of page header, the small label at the start of each page. Sorting changed nothing in the data and made the status column about 250 times smaller.

sections.h: The footer's smallest and largest values let a reader skip whole row groups
sections.html:
A fraud analyst, someone who hunts for stolen cards, wants every payment above 1,500 euros: WHERE amount_cents > 150000. Column pruning, reading only the columns a query names, already lets the reader skip payment_id and card_country. Can it skip rows too, before reading them?

It can, with the footer. Next to each chunk's offset and size, the footer stores the smallest and largest value in that chunk, its min and max. Think back to the moving boxes: the footer is the label from every box, all copied onto one sheet. Look at the sorted file from the first Try it. Row group 0 holds amounts from 100 to 63,031 cents. No row in it can be above 150,000, so the reader skips the whole row group, every column of it, without reading a byte of its data. Row group 1 tops out at 125,677, so it's skipped too. Row groups 2 and 3 might hold matches, so the reader fetches them. The stepper below walks through it.

Skipping data by checking a filter against these numbers, inside the file reader, is called predicate pushdown. A predicate is a condition such as amount_cents > 150000. Pushing it down means handing it from the query to the reader, which compares it with every row group's min and max. Databases that store by column keep the same numbers and call them zone maps; Column stores and compression met them.

Min and max describe a range, not the values inside it. A row group whose amounts run from 100 to 250,099 might hold a payment of 240,000 cents, so the reader must open it. That's why the order of the rows decides everything. The two demo files hold the same 400,000 payments. In the random file, written in payment order, every row group spans almost the whole range, 100 to about 250,000. That's the friend who wrote "books" on every box. In the sorted file, each row group covers its own quarter of the range.

The next Try it runs amount_cents > 240000 on both files. On the sorted file, Spark reads one row group of four. On the random file, it reads all four, and the filter throws away 96% of those rows afterwards.

Min and max skip only what sorting made tidy. Sort each file by the column you filter on most. The worked example in Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore sorted each day's rows by shop for exactly this reason. One sort can make only one column tidy, though: the sorted file's merchant_id chunks still run from 0 to 499 in every row group.

The moving boxes break in one place. You can repack a box when you notice the mess, while a Parquet file is never changed once it's written. To tidy one, you write a new file.

Pushdown also needs a reader that uses it. Spark's Parquet reader does (spark.sql.parquet.filterPushdown is on by default), and so does DuckDB's. But a filter that Spark hands to the reader doesn't always skip anything. Next, we'll catch it failing.

try.title: The same filter on sorted and random rows
steps: From the labs folder, run SkippingDemo. It runs one query against the sorted file and the random file, in Spark and in DuckDB. Spark reports how many rows its scan, the step that reads the file, handed on; DuckDB reports how many bytes it read.
Predict first: the sorted file's row groups start at 100, 63,033, 125,677 and 188,241 cents. How many rows will Spark's scan unpack for amount_cents > 240000?
Compare the bytes DuckDB read from each file. Which chunks make up the smaller number?

code.title: SkippingDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l05.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col /** * The same filter on the same 400,000 payments, stored sorted by amount and in random order. * Spark reports how many rows its scan handed on; DuckDB reports how many bytes it read. */ fun main() { PaymentParquet.open().use { duck -> val spark = demoSpark() println("SELECT merchant_id, amount_cents WHERE amount_cents > 240000") for (file in listOf(PaymentParquet.sorted, PaymentParquet.random)) { val query = spark.read().parquet(file.absolutePath) .where(col("amount_cents").gt(240_000)) .select("merchant_id", "amount_cents") val matching = query.collectAsList().size if (file == PaymentParquet.sorted) println("Spark's PushedFilters: [${pushedFilters(query)}]") val profile = duck.rows("EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT merchant_id, amount_cents FROM '${file.absolutePath}' WHERE amount_cents > 240000") .joinToString("\n") { it[1] ?: "" } val read = Regex("""Data Read:\s*([\d.]+ [kMG]?B)""").find(profile)?.groupValues?.get(1) println("%-15s Spark scan handed on %,7d rows, %,d match. DuckDB read %s".format(file.name, scanRows(query), matching, read)) } spark.stop() } }

try.expect:
SELECT merchant_id, amount_cents WHERE amount_cents > 240000
Spark's PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount_cents), GreaterThan(amount_cents,240000)]
sorted.parquet  Spark scan handed on  98,944 rows, 16,200 match.  DuckDB read 382.7 kB
random.parquet  Spark scan handed on 400,000 rows, 16,200 match.  DuckDB read 2.3 MB

Both files give the same 16,200 rows. On the sorted file, Spark's scan unpacked 98,944 rows, exactly row group 3, and DuckDB read 383 kB, most of it the two chunks of that row group (113,895 + 252,426 bytes). On the random file, the scan unpacked all 400,000 rows and DuckDB read about 2.3 MB, six times more for the same answer. The 2.3 MB moves a little between runs.

sections.h: When a filter looks pushed down and still reads everything
sections.html:
Spark tells you what it pushed. Ask it with explain(), which prints its plan, the list of steps it will run. For the query above, the line about reading the file says:

FileScan parquet [merchant_id#1,amount_cents#4L] ...
  PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount_cents), GreaterThan(amount_cents,240000)],
  ReadSchema: struct<merchant_id:int,amount_cents:bigint>

ReadSchema is column pruning: the reader will unpack two columns. PushedFilters is the filter Spark handed to the reader. Here's the catch: it's a list of what Spark asked for, not of what the file could skip. There are three common ways to get a long PushedFilters list and skip nothing.

First, a function around the column. WHERE date_format(created_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd') = '2026-11-07' turns each payment's time (created_at) into a piece of text, then compares the text. The footer has min and max for created_at, not for that text, so Spark pushes only IsNotNull(created_at) and reads every row group. Write the filter on the raw column instead: created_at >= '2026-11-07' AND created_at < '2026-11-08'.

Second, data that isn't sorted by the column. merchant_id = 42 is pushed in full, but every row group holds shops 0 to 499, so the min and max never rule one out. It's the box labelled "books" again.

Third, a column without statistics, the min and max a writer stores. This one surprises people. Spark 4.1 still writes times in an old type called INT96 by default (the setting is spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType), and parquet-java keeps no min or max for INT96 columns. So a time filter on a file Spark wrote with its default settings shows up in PushedFilters and skips nothing. Set the type to TIMESTAMP_MICROS, the standard one, and the same filter on the same rows skips about five of every six row groups.

All three run correctly and return the right rows, so nobody notices the full read. The way to know is to measure: compare the rows the scan handed on with the rows in the table. Spark shows them as "number of output rows" on the scan, in the SQL tab of the Spark UI. That's the web page every Spark program serves while it runs, and lesson 6 opens it. In DuckDB, EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and reports the bytes each step read.

PushedFilters lists what Spark asked for. Count what the scan read.

Min and max can't help with one more case: finding one value among millions of unsorted ones, such as one reference code. Parquet has two optional extras for that. A bloom filter per column chunk is a small pattern of bits that answers "could this value be here?" with "no" or "maybe". parquet-java leaves bloom filters off by default; DuckDB 2.0 wrote them for the demo file's dictionary columns. The page index stores min and max for every page, near the footer, so a reader can skip pages inside a row group it has to open.

That's everything one file lets a reader skip. What happens between your query and these files, across many machines at once, is Spark's work, and the next lesson opens it up.

code.title: PushdownDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l05.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Column import org.apache.spark.sql.SaveMode import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.date_format import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.hash import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.lit import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.pmod import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.timestamp_seconds import java.io.File /** * Spark writes a week of 200,000 payments sorted by created_at, in small row groups, twice: with * its default timestamp type (INT96) and with TIMESTAMP_MICROS. Then it runs four filters and * prints what it pushed to the Parquet reader and how many rows the scan handed on. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() spark.conf().set("spark.sql.maxMetadataStringLength", "400") // print PushedFilters in full val payments = spark.range(0, 200_000, 1, 4).select( col("id").alias("payment_id"), pmod(hash(col("id")), lit(500)).alias("merchant_id"), pmod(hash(col("id"), lit(2)), lit(250_000)).plus(100).cast("bigint").alias("amount_cents"), // a random second in the week starting 2026-11-01 00:00 UTC timestamp_seconds(lit(1_793_491_200L).plus(pmod(hash(col("id"), lit(3)), lit(7 * 86_400)))).alias("created_at"), ) val files = mutableMapOf<String, String>() for (type in listOf("TIMESTAMP_MICROS", "INT96")) { spark.conf().set("spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType", type) val dir = File("build/l04/by-time-$type").absolutePath payments.repartition(1).sortWithinPartitions("created_at") .write().mode(SaveMode.Overwrite).option("parquet.block.size", 256 * 1024).parquet(dir) files[type] = dir } val fromNov7 = col("created_at").geq(lit("2026-11-07 00:00:00").cast("timestamp")) val cases = listOf<Triple<String, String, Column>>( Triple("created_at >= '2026-11-07'", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS", fromNov7), Triple("date_format(created_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd') = '2026-11-07'", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS", date_format(col("created_at"), "yyyy-MM-dd").equalTo("2026-11-07")), Triple("merchant_id = 42", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS", col("merchant_id").equalTo(42)), Triple("created_at >= '2026-11-07'", "INT96", fromNov7), ) for ((label, type, filter) in cases) { val query = spark.read().parquet(files.getValue(type)).where(filter) val matching = query.collectAsList().size println("WHERE $label ($type file)") println(" PushedFilters: [${pushedFilters(query)}]") println(" scan handed on %,d of 200,000 rows; %,d match".format(scanRows(query), matching)) } spark.stop() }

The second query returns the same rows and reads everything. The third pushes its filter and still reads everything. opening:
Picture moving house. You pack your books into twenty boxes and label each one: "books, authors A to C". To find a cookbook by Moreno, you open one box. A friend packed hers in any order and labelled every box "books". She opens all twenty.

Data files have the same problem. Ask for every payment above 2,400 euros from two files that hold the same 400,000 payments. The reader fetches 383 kB from one and 2.3 MB from the other, for the same 16,200 rows. Only the order of the rows differs.

It's easy to believe that a file stored by column reads only the rows a question needs. It reads only the columns it needs, and skips rows only when the labels prove they can't match.

In Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore, a query skipped whole days by their directory names. In this lesson, we'll go inside the files: design one, read one from the back, and catch filters that look like they skip and don't. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two files holding the same 400,000 payments, where one question fetched six times more from one than from the other. Both files had a label on every row group. In the file written in payment order, every label said "anything". Sorting the rows made each label narrow, and the reader skipped three row groups of four.

If you have DuckDB, run SELECT row_group_id, path_in_schema, stats_min, stats_max FROM parquet_metadata('build/l04/random.parquet') in the labs/bigdata folder after the Try its. Then run it on sorted.parquet, and compare the ranges for amount_cents.

Next, we'll meet Spark properly, and find out how it turns one query into many small pieces of work spread across machines.

drill.title: Skip from the footer
drill.prompt: From memory, write the three decisions a Parquet reader makes before it reads any data: find the footer's length from the end of the file, decide whether a column chunk with a given min and max may hold a value between lo and hi, and add up the bytes it will fetch for a set of columns in a set of row groups.

answer.html: fun footerLength(file: File): Int = RandomAccessFile(file, "r").use { f -> f.seek(f.length() - 8) // [length: 4 bytes LE][PAR1] val tail = ByteArray(8).also { f.readFully(it) } require(String(tail, 4, 4, Charsets.US_ASCII) == "PAR1") ByteBuffer.wrap(tail, 0, 4).order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).int } fun mayContain(min: Long?, max: Long?, lo: Long, hi: Long): Boolean = min == null || max == null || (max >= lo && min <= hi) // no stats: must read fun bytesToRead(groups: List<RowGroup>, keep: List<Int>, columns: Set<String>): Long = groups.filter { it.index in keep } .sumOf { g -> columns.sumOf { g.columns.getValue(it).bytes } }

recap: A Parquet file is row groups (slices of rows), each holding one column chunk per column, then a footer, a 4-byte footer length and PAR1. The footer comes last, so the writer needs only one pass.
A reader reads the last 8 bytes, then the footer, then only the chunks it needs, each as one byte range.

Encodings shrink a column using its values: a dictionary turns 4 statuses into 2-bit codes, sorting turns those into long runs, and delta encoding stores differences. Snappy or Zstd then compress the result.
The footer's min and max per chunk let a reader skip whole row groups: predicate pushdown. It works only when the rows are sorted, or grouped, by the filter column.

The limit: PushedFilters lists what Spark offered the reader, not what it skipped. A function around the column, unsorted data and INT96 times (Spark's default) all skip nothing. Measure the rows the scan read.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Parquet stores data by column, so our time-range queries only read the rows they need." Explain what Parquet really lets a reader skip, and what has to be true for a time filter to skip anything.
explain.answer: Parquet lets a reader skip two things before it unpacks any data. It skips columns, because each row group stores each column as its own chunk and the footer says where every chunk is. That's column pruning, and it always works. It can also skip whole row groups, because the footer stores each chunk's min and max. A time filter skips a row group only when that row group's min and max for the time column prove that no row can match. So three things must be true. The column needs min and max values, which Spark's default INT96 times don't get, so write TIMESTAMP_MICROS. The rows must be sorted or grouped by time, or every row group spans the whole day and nothing is ruled out. And the filter must be on the raw column, not wrapped in a function like date_format. Inside the row groups it does read, the reader unpacks every row and a filter drops the ones that don't match, so it never reads only the matching rows.

deeper.html:
Parquet has two older relatives you'll meet in older systems. ORC came out of the Hive project with the same idea under different names: a file is a series of stripes (row groups), each with a stream per column, indexes holding min and max, and a footer at the end. Hive tables were often ORC, and Spark, Trino and DuckDB all read it. Avro is the opposite, a row format. It stores each record whole, one after another, and writes the schema once at the top of the file. That suits writing one event at a time. It's why Avro is common for messages in Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages for other programs to read, and why Iceberg (lesson 11) keeps its manifest files, its lists of data files, in Avro. For questions about a few columns of many rows, Avro reads every byte, like a CSV file.

One more detail of the footer is worth knowing: min and max for text. parquet-java can shorten long min and max strings (parquet.statistics.truncate.length, and 64 bytes for the page index by default). When it shortens the max, it rounds it up, so the range still covers the real values. A shortened range is wider than the true one, so it can only cause extra reads, never wrong answers. That rule holds for all of pushdown: min and max may make a reader read too much, never too little, because the filter above the scan still checks every row it gets.
